lessons.title: Estimate the Percent of a Number
lessons.objective: I can estimate the percent of a number using benchmark percents, rounding, and compatible numbers.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain an estimate using the words about, benchmark, and compatible numbers.

concept.heading: Approximately — the problem is asking for an estimate
concept.intro: The word approximately tells you an exact answer is not required. Benchmarks, rounding and compatible numbers get you close, fast.
concept.keyIdea: Estimating Percents of Numbers. 1. Use benchmark percents: 10% (move decimal left 1), 1% (move left 2), 50% (half), 25% (quarter). 2. Combine benchmarks (e.g. 15% = 10% + 5%; 75% = 50% + 25%). 3. Round numbers to compatible values for quick mental estimates

worked.title: Watch me set up the double number line
lines: The whole is 6 GB — that is 100%.
I mark the bottom line in benchmark jumps of 25%: 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%.
Equivalent ratios give the top line: 25% of 6 GB is 1.5 GB, so the top reads 0, 1.5, 3, 4.5, 6.
4 GB used lands between 4.5 (75%) and 3 (50%), close to 4.5 — so about 70% of the storage is used.
linesEs: El entero es 6 GB — eso es el 100%.
Marco la línea de abajo en saltos de referencia de 25%: 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%.
Las razones equivalentes dan la línea de arriba: el 25% de 6 GB es 1.5 GB, así que arriba se lee 0, 1.5, 3, 4.5, 6.
Los 4 GB usados caen entre 4.5 (75%) y 3 (50%), cerca de 4.5 — así que se usa como el 70% del almacenamiento.
worked.titleEs: Mírame armar la recta numérica doble

together.title: Let's estimate the metal recycling together
lines: The Green-Team recycled 216 pounds of material; 8.6% was metal.
Round both: 8.6% is about 10%, and 216 is about 220.
Compatible numbers work too: 10% of 200 = 20. Both estimates agree — around 20 pounds.
linesEs: El Equipo Verde recicló 216 libras de material; el 8.6% era metal.
Redondea los dos: 8.6% es como 10%, y 216 es como 220.
El 10% de 220 = 0.1 × 220 = 22. Unas 22 libras de metal.
Los números compatibles también sirven: el 10% de 200 = 20. Las dos estimaciones coinciden — alrededor de 20 libras.
together.titleEs: Estimemos juntos el reciclaje de metal

vocabulary.definition: A reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful, found without exact computation.
A friendly percent — 1%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% — used as a landmark for estimating.
vocabulary.example: 1% · 10% · 25% · 50% · 75% · 100% — the landmarks you can find mentally.

vocabulary.definition: Numbers close to the originals that are easy to compute with mentally.
vocabulary.example: 8.6% of 216 → 10% of 220: both nudged to numbers that divide nicely.

vocabulary.definition: Two parallel number lines that pair amounts with their percents at the same positions.
The quantity that counts as 100% in a problem — and it can change between questions.
vocabulary.example: “Of the USED storage” makes 4 GB the whole — not the 6 GB total.

vocabulary.definition: Break a percent into friendly pieces that are easy to find.

lessons.title: Find and Compare with Percentages
lessons.objective: I can find the percent of a number using an equation or a model.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my steps using the words percent, base, part, and equation.

concept.heading: How do I find the percent of a number?
concept.intro: A percent is a piece of a whole. The whole is called the base — it is the number right after the word “of,” and “of” means multiply. Your answer is the piece you get, called the part.
concept.keyIdea: Finding the Percent of a Number. Formula: Part = Percent × Whole. 1. Identify the percent and the whole (base amount). 2. Convert the percent to a decimal or simplified fraction. 3. Multiply the decimal/fraction by the whole to calculate the part

worked.title: Watch me
lines: The claw machine costs 60 tickets, and it is 25% off. I need 25% of 60.
Step 1 — find the base (the whole): the number after “of” is 60.
Step 2 — the percent as a decimal: 25% means 25 out of 100, so 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25.
The discount is 15 tickets. Check: 15 is about a quarter of 60, so that makes sense.
linesEs: La máquina de garra cuesta 60 boletos, y tiene 25% de descuento. Necesito el 25% de 60.
Paso 1 — halla la base (el entero): el número después de «de» es 60.
Paso 2 — el porcentaje como decimal: 25% significa 25 de cada 100, así que 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25.
El descuento es de 15 boletos. Comprueba: 15 es como la cuarta parte de 60, así que tiene sentido.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Find 40% of 80. Step 1 — what is the base? (80, the number after “of”)
Does 32 make sense? 40% is a little less than half, and half of 80 is 40. ✓
linesEs: Halla el 40% de 80. Paso 1 — ¿cuál es la base? (80, el número después de «de»)
¿Tiene sentido 32? El 40% es un poco menos de la mitad, y la mitad de 80 es 40. ✓

vocabulary.definition: A part of a number found by multiplying the number by the percent written as a decimal.
A way to compare a number to 100, shown with the % sign.
The whole amount you start with — the number right after the word “of.”
How much of the base (the whole) you get. It is your answer.
vocabulary.example: 25% of 80 = 20 → the part is 20 (20 out of the 80).

vocabulary.definition: A number sentence with an equal sign. The percent one is: part = percent × base.
Money taken off the first price to make it cheaper.
Two number lines that line up percents with amounts.
vocabulary.example: 0%–100% on one line over 0–300 on the other.

vocabulary.definition: A fraction with the same value written with different numbers.

investigate: Find 10%, 25%, and 50% of the same price using benchmarks.

Explain why a 25% discount is not the same as subtracting $25 from every price.
create: Create a truthful sale sign with original price, percent discount, dollars saved, and final price. Show a benchmark estimate and explain the calculation.

support.prompt: Margaret's phone has 6 GB of storage and 4 GB is used. About what percent is used?
support.explanation: 4 out of 6 is 2/3, which is about 67%, so 'about 70%' is the reasonable estimate.
feedback: 25% of 6 GB would be only 1.5 GB.
That reads the 4 GB as 40% — but the whole is 6, not 10.
More than 100% would mean using more storage than the phone has.
hints: What is the whole?
4 out of 6 is the same as 2 out of 3.
Two-thirds is close to which benchmark?

support.prompt: On the double number line for 6 GB, what amount lines up with 25%?
support.explanation: 25% of 6 GB is one quarter of 6, which is 1.5 GB.
feedback: That divides 6 by 4.8 rather than by 4.
2.5 GB would be more than a third of the storage.
4 GB lines up near 67%, not 25%.
hints: 25% means one quarter.
One quarter of 6.

support.prompt: Which benchmark percents make good landmarks on a number line?
support.explanation: Multiples of 25 (and 10) are friendly landmarks because their amounts are easy to compute.
feedback: Those percents are no easier to compute with than the original problem.
50% alone leaves most of the line unmarked.
100% alone gives you nothing to compare against in the middle.
hints: Which percents can you find mentally?
Quarters and tenths are the friendly ones.

support.prompt: To estimate 8.6% of 216 by rounding, which numbers should you use?
support.explanation: 8.6% rounds to 10% and 216 rounds to 220 — both are close to the originals and easy to compute.
feedback: 1% is far below 8.6%, so the estimate would be far too small.
300 is far from 216, so the estimate drifts too far.
86% misplaces the decimal — that is ten times too large.
hints: Round each number to something friendly.
8.6% is close to which benchmark?
216 is close to which round number?

support.prompt: The word 'approximately' appears in the storage problem. What does it tell you about the answer you need?
support.explanation: It tells me an exact answer is not required — I can use benchmarks and rounding to get close, and 'about 70%' counts as correct.

feedback: Multiply 150 by 0.20, or divide by 5.
Not quite. Multiply: 0.20 × 150 = ___.
Try converting 20% to a decimal or fraction first.
hints: '20% of 150' means you want a PART of 150 — the answer should be smaller than 150.
Convert the percent to a decimal, then multiply: Part = Percent × Base.
Write 20% as 0.20, then set up 0.20 × 150. (Shortcut: 10% of 150 is 15 — double it.)

feedback: That is what you get if you subtracted 50 from 84. Instead: Multiply: 0.50 × 84 = ___.
50% is half — divide 84 by 2.
Not quite. Multiply: 0.50 × 84 = ___.
hints: 50% is a friendly percent — it means exactly one-half of the number.
Finding 50% of a number is the same as dividing that number by 2.
Set up 84 ÷ 2, or check with the formula: 0.50 × 84.

support.explanation: 10% = 0.10. Multiply: 0.10 × 320 = 32. (Or move the decimal one place left.)
feedback: 10% is one-tenth — divide 320 by 10 or move the decimal.
10% is easy: just divide by 10.
Not quite. Multiply: 0.10 × 320 = ___.
hints: 10% means one-tenth — there's a shortcut that needs no multiplication at all.
To find 10% of any number, move the decimal point one place to the left (divide by 10).
Start with 320 and slide the decimal one place left: 320 → what number?

feedback: Scale 15/50 to a denominator of 100: 50 × 2 = 100, so the top doubles too.
Set it up as a fraction: 15/50, then rebuild it out of 100.
Find what fraction 15 is of 50, then convert.
hints: This question is backwards from the others: you have the part (15) and the whole (50), and you need the PERCENT.
Write the part over the whole as a fraction, then rebuild it as a fraction out of 100 — percent means out of 100.
Set up 15/50. What times 50 gives 100? (2) So multiply the top by 2 as well: 15 × 2 = 30 → 30/100.

support.explanation: First change the percent to a decimal: 30% = 30 ÷ 100 = 0.30. Then multiply by the base: 0.30 × 80 = 24. So 30% of 80 = 24, not 2,400. The student multiplied by 30 instead of 0.30.
hints: A percent is not a whole number — change 30% to a decimal before you multiply.
30% = 0.30. Multiply 0.30 × 80 to find the part: 24.

support.explanation: 25% of 80 = 20. Final price: $60. The discount is subtracted from the original price.

core.prompt: The Green-Team recycled 216 pounds; 8.6% was metal. Using compatible numbers 10% and 200, the estimate is:
feedback: That is 1% of 200 — the decimal moved one place too far.
That reads 8.6% as 86 pounds.
That subtracts 8 from 216 instead of taking a percent.
hints: Write 10% as a decimal.
One tenth of 200.

core.prompt: Photos use 3.5 GB of the 4 GB of used storage. About what percent of the USED storage is photos?
core.explanation: The whole is 4 GB here. 75% of 4 is 3 GB and 100% is 4 GB; 3.5 sits midway — about 87%.
feedback: That reads 3.5 GB as 35% — the whole is 4, not 10.
That uses 6 GB as the whole, but the question asks about the USED storage.
3.5 out of 4 is clearly below 100%, but not that close to it.
hints: What is the whole for THIS question?
The whole is 4 GB, not 6.
3.5 of 4 is between the 75% and 100% marks.

core.prompt: Margaret has a 6 GB phone with 4 GB used. Question A asks what percent of the total 6 GB is used. Question B asks what percent of the used 4 GB is photos. Why is the whole different in the two questions?
choices: The phone gained storage between the questions
The whole never changes in a percent problem
The second question asks about the used storage, so 4 GB becomes 100%
Because photos are more important than mail
core.explanation: Each percent question defines its own whole. 'Of the used storage' makes the 4 GB the new 100%.
feedback: The phone's capacity never changed — the QUESTION changed.
The whole is set by the question, and this pair of questions sets it differently.
Importance has nothing to do with which quantity is the whole.
hints: Re-read: 'Of the USED storage…'
Which quantity is that question about?
That quantity becomes 100%.

core.explanation: 24% is about 25%, and 81 is about 80. One quarter of 80 is 20.
feedback: 2 is about 2.5% of 81 — far below 24%.
8 is about 10% of 81, not 24%.
40 would be about half of 81, but 24% is about a quarter.
hints: Which benchmark is 24% near?
25% is one quarter.
One quarter of 80.

core.prompt: Estimate 47% of 312. Show which strategy you used — benchmark, rounding, or compatible numbers — and give your estimate.
core.explanation: 47% is about 50%, and 312 is about 300. Half of 300 is 150, so 47% of 312 is about 150. I used a benchmark (50%) with a compatible number (300).

core.prompt: An arcade prize costs 240 tickets. If you have a coupon for 15% off, how many tickets do you save?
feedback: Make sure you're subtracting the discount from the total.
Find the discount amount, then subtract from the original.
Not quite. 15% of 240 = 0.15 × 240 = ___ tickets saved.
hints: Read carefully: the question asks how many tickets you SAVE — that's just the discount amount, not the new price.
The savings = 15% of the original 240 tickets. Convert 15% to a decimal and multiply.
Set up 0.15 × 240. (Shortcut: 10% of 240 is 24, and 5% is half of that — add them.)

core.prompt: A student scored 72 out of 90 on a test. What percent did they score?
feedback: Simplify 72/90 to 8/10, then scale it to a denominator of 100.
Convert to a fraction first: 72/90, then rebuild it out of 100.
Find what fraction 72 is of 90, then convert to percent.
hints: The score 72 is the part and 90 is the whole — you need what percent 72 is OF 90.
Write the part over the whole, then rebuild it as a fraction out of 100 — percent means out of 100.
Set up 72/90 and simplify first: both divide by 9 → 8/10. Now 10 × 10 = 100, so 8 × 10 = 80 → 80/100.

steps: Change the percent to a decimal: 15% = 0.15
core.explanation: The base is 60, not 15. The word "of" tells you the base: 15% OF 60. Multiply by the base: 0.15 × 60 = 9. So 15% of 60 = 9, not 2.25. The student multiplied by the percent number instead of the base.
hints: What number comes after the word "of"? That is the base you multiply by.
15% = 0.15, and the base is 60. Multiply 0.15 × 60 = 9.

stretch.prompt: Two students estimate 8.6% of 216. Ana uses 10% of 220 = 22. Ben uses 10% of 200 = 20. Whose estimate is closer to the exact answer, 18.576?
choices: Ben's — 20 is 1.4 away; Ana's 22 is 3.4 away
stretch.explanation: Exact is 18.576. Ben's 20 misses by about 1.4; Ana's 22 misses by about 3.4. Compatible numbers won this one.
feedback: 22 − 18.576 = 3.424, which is farther than Ben's 1.424.
The two distances are 1.4 and 3.4 — not equal.
Both are valid estimates; the question is which lands closer.
hints: Find each distance from 18.576.
1.4 versus 3.4.

stretch.prompt: For which problem is ESTIMATING clearly the right tool, rather than exact computation?
choices: Deciding if a $58 jacket at 25% off fits your $45 budget
Programming a bank to compute interest on every account
stretch.explanation: A quick benchmark — 25% of 60 is 15, so about $43 — answers the budget question; the others need exactness.
feedback: Bank interest must be computed exactly, to the cent.
Medicine doses can never be 'about right'.
Test scoring has to be exact for every student.
hints: Where is 'close enough' good enough?
Money decisions you make in an aisle are estimates.
The other three carry real risk if inexact.

stretch.prompt: A store marks a $79.95 item 32% off. Which mental estimate best checks the discount?
choices: About one third of 80, so about $26 off
stretch.explanation: 32% is near the benchmark 1/3, and $79.95 is nearly 80. A third of 80 is about 26.7.
feedback: That is 4% of 80, a misplaced decimal.
Percent is not a dollar count — 32% of 80 is not automatically $32 (though here it lands nearby, the reasoning is wrong).
Half would be 50%, far above 32%.
hints: Which fraction benchmark is 32% near?
One third.
A third of 80.

stretch.prompt: Write your own estimation problem about percent, using a real situation from your life. Then solve it with a benchmark and say whether your estimate runs high or low.
stretch.explanation: My playlist has 62 songs and about 48% are hip-hop. 48% is about 50%, and 62 is about 60, so about 30 songs. Both roundings moved in opposite directions, so my estimate is very close.
30% = 0.30 (divide by 100, not by 10). 0.30 × 90 = 27. The correct answer is 27.
hints: To convert a percent to a decimal, divide by 100 — how many places does the decimal move?
30% = 0.30, not 3.0. The student divided by 10 instead of 100.

stretch.prompt: A class has 32 students. 25% are in the math club, 50% are in the reading club, and 12.5% are in both. How many students are in each group? Can the total of all three groups be more than 32? Explain why or why not.
stretch.frame: There are ___ in math club, ___ in reading club, and ___ in both. The total ___ be more than 32 because ___.
stretch.explanation: Taking each percent of the same 32 students gives 25% = 32 ÷ 4 = 8 in math club, 50% = 32 ÷ 2 = 16 in reading club, and 12.5% = 32 ÷ 8 = 4 in both. Adding 8 + 16 + 4 = 28 is misleading, because the 4 students in both are already inside the 8 and the 16 — counting them a third time overlaps, and the number of different students in at least one club is 8 + 16 − 4 = 20.
hints: There are three separate percents of the SAME 32 students: 25%, 50%, and 12.5%. Find each group first.
Use friendly fractions: 25% = 1/4, 50% = 1/2, and 12.5% = 1/8. Then think about students who got counted in two groups.
Start with 25% of 32: that's 32 ÷ 4. Then do 32 ÷ 2 and 32 ÷ 8, and think about the 'both clubs' overlap.
